articles.title: Indian Army Launches Bharat Rice for Troops in Presence of Defence Minister
articles.text:
The Indian Army launched ‘Bharat Rice’ for the defence forces, at a ceremony graced by Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh and Minister of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution Shri Pralhad Joshi in New Delhi on October 12, 2026. The event also featured the signing of an MoU between the Indian Army and Food Corporation of India (FCI) for utilisation of its infrastructure during operational contingencies. This superior quality rice will be delivered directly to Army Supply Depots, including those in far-flung areas of Ladakh and the North East, instead of being collected by Army depots from local FCI facilities.
In his address, Raksha Mantri described ‘Bharat Rice’ as a bond of trust that begins in the farmer’s field and extends to the soldier’s plate. He stated that the initiative provides a tangible form to the spirit of ‘Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan’ as it embodies a collective resolve where the hard work of a farmer transforms into the strength of a soldier. “This superior-quality rice will be provided in accordance with standard specifications. Furthermore, we are ensuring ergonomic packaging. While this initiative might appear small, it offers immense operational relief to the soldiers responsible for transporting rations to remote and difficult terrains,” he added.
Shri Rajnath Singh emphasised that the soldiers’ operational readiness is not defined by weaponry alone; it also lies in their physical health, mental balance, morale and stamina, especially as they serve in harshest of conditions. He termed the welfare of soldiers as not a peripheral issue, but an integral component of national security, adding that healthy food, robust equipment and complete training boost the morale of troops, making them ready to face every challenge, and protect the nation.
Raksha Mantri asserted that in modern-day warfare, weapons, platforms, and technology are not the only critical elements; logistics itself is combat power. He stated that wars today are not won solely on the front lines, and factors such as the strength of supply chains, storage capacity, transportation networks, warehousing infrastructure, and the ability for timely replenishment play an equally crucial role.
“The strategic analysis of Operation Sindoor indicated that warning times could be extremely short in future conflicts. Scenarios involving zero-warning situations and the integration of technology into warfare could severely test our preparedness. Such conflicts could also put the endurance of our logistics chains and supply networks to the test. Therefore, we must build logistics resilience to sustain our operations. This MoU with FCI represents a significant step in that direction,” said Shri Rajnath Singh.
Raksha Mantri added that FCI possesses warehouses, storage infrastructure, modern silos, material handling equipment, and trained manpower across the country, including the operationally significant areas. This initiative is proof that the country’s existing national capacity can be aligned with national security requirements when the need arises, he said, adding that it represents a dual-use approach, wherein the country’s infrastructure and capabilities serve not just a single purpose, but cater to both civil and military needs.
Shri Rajnath Singh underlined that just as fighter aircraft are now landing on expressways, and roads & bridges built by Border Roads Organisation are being utilised by local residents too, FCI godowns will no longer be limited to food storage; they will become an integral part of the Indian Army’s supply chain. “This approach will optimise resources and strengthen national resilience. Integrating existing infrastructure with operational planning allows us to save time and utilise resources more effectively. This MoU is far more than a mere administrative arrangement. It acts as a force multiplier for operational preparedness and reflects our ‘Whole-of-Government’ and ‘Whole-of-Nation’ approach,” he said.
Raksha Mantri highlighted the Government’s focus on every aspect of our soldiers’ welfare, adding that emphasis has been placed on self-reliance and modernisation across all sectors, from weaponry and technology to clothing, equipment, and training. “Today, India produces a significant portion of its defence requirements domestically,” he said, underlining that innovation and coordination are the basis of the Government’s resolve to continuously provide best quality products to the soldiers, make the supply chains more resilient, ensure timely deliveries to forward areas, and better utilise civilian infrastructure for national security. He added that when the soldiers stand guard at the borders, they must have the confidence that the entire country stands with them. He termed boosting the morale of soldiers as the Government’s priority, emphasising that this resolve is not of the government alone; it is shared by the farmers, the cooperative sector, the civil administration, and the nation at large.
Speaking on the occasion, Minister of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution Shri Pralhad Joshi appreciated the ‘Bharat Rice’ initiative, and said that it is a matter of pride for his department to provide superior quality rice to those who protect the nation with unmatched bravery and dedication. “To provide quality food to the nation’s protectors and cater to their needs is our duty,” he said.
Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth, Secretary (Food and Public Distribution) Shri Sanjeev Chopra and senior officials from the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, FCI, National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Limited (NAFED) and the cooperative sector were present on the occasion.
About Bharat Rice
Spearheaded by the Directorate General of Supplies and Transport, the Bharat Rice initiative is based on sustained feedback from troops and is aimed at improving the quality of rations. The rice will be milled to prescribed defence specifications and supplied through NAFED during Financial Year 2026-27. It will undergo requisite quality-control checks and will be free from foreign matter and admixtures, with minimal broken, damaged and discoloured grains.
Procurement in 10 kg and 30 kg bags will further ease handling and transportation, particularly at forward posts. The initiative follows nearly 18 months of coordination among the Army, FCI, NAFED and the Department of Food & Public Distribution.
The MoU with FCI draws upon operational lessons, including those from Operation Sindoor, which highlighted the requirement for resilient logistics arrangements during contingencies that may arise at short notice and extend over prolonged periods. It provides the Indian Army a formal framework to utilise identified FCI warehousing infrastructure, labour resources and material-handling equipment during operational contingencies.
Coordination will be undertaken at formation level between the Army’s Supply and Transport elements and FCI’s Regional and Divisional Offices and integrated into operational logistics plans. The MoU will remain valid for five years, extendable by mutual consent.
The arrangement will enable additional storage, rapid mobilisation, dispersion and forward positioning of rations, stores and equipment closer to operational areas, thereby strengthening the responsiveness and resilience of military logistics while optimising existing national infrastructure. The initiative reflects a whole-of-government approach aligned with the vision of PM Gati Shakti.
The Indian Army has also undertaken a series of measures in recent years to improve ration quality and scales, including additional rations for Agniveer recruits and greater commonality in ration scales across the three Services. Organic rations are also proposed to be introduced.
articles.summary: The Indian Army launched ‘Bharat Rice’ for the defence forces, at a ceremony graced by Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh and Minister of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution Shri Pralhad Joshi

articles.title: India’s Rafale Production to Focus on Keeping More Jets Mission-Ready
articles.text:
The Indian-made Rafale F-4 Plus will include a clause that will make it mandatory for the Dassault Indian partner to supply and maintain readiness of 75% of the fleet availability to ensure that out of 114 jets, nearly 85 jets can be operated by the IAF.
idw has been told that the same deal was also part of the previous Rafale purchase, where Dassault had to ensure that a fleet availability rate of 75% and above was maintained so that even in case of high operation ratio requirements, at least 27 of the Rafale fleet is ready for operations.
IAF will be getting at least 10 years of direct support, but it seems that, with Rafale being made locally in the country, it will be tasked as the local partner in the program . It has been reported that IAF, with a fleet of 36 aircraft, was able to maintain 80-90% serviceability .
While France has struggled to maintain such serviceability in its own operations, Dassault officals told idrw that the airframe was designed for it and, due to its modular line replaceable units that can be swapped in minutes and no runway test bences requuired their is no need for long periodic airframe overhauls that cut down time on the airframe side.
But the real constraint issue was the support chain that includes spares and M-88 engine overhauls and deep maintenance that has directly improved the serviceability of the aircraft . Each Rafale costs roughly €2.7–3.5 million a year to keep in condition (about ₹25–33 crore), consumes 30–32 maintenance man-hours per flight hour, and runs ~$16,000–20,000 per flight hour.
Engine overhaul has been planned to take place in Hyderabad, and local MRO support has also been planned; along with that, Dassault also has plans to allow most of the spares to be locally manufactured here in the country, for which it is also in talks with indian aerospace companies. Indian depot-level facility that will be managed by the IAF has also been planned to meet demanding serviceability requirements that will be in the contract that is now likely to happen by the end of this year.
RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.text: New Delhi: The Harvard Club of India has clarified that it has neither issued nor endorsed any statement concerning the recent protests in New Delhi and the actions taken by authorities in connection with the agitation against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Rajat Sethi, an Executive Committee member of the Harvard Club of India, clarified the organisation's position while speaking to ANI."As a member of the elected body of the Executive Council of the Harvard Club of India, which is the official alumni group of Harvard University alumni in India, I wanted to issue a clarification that certain individuals have gone ahead and issued a letter remarking on and making comments about the recent protest and the detention that followed. I wanted to issue a clarification that this is not the official position of the Harvard Club of India," Sethi said.He further said that the Club's charter and mandate prohibit it from issuing political statements on its own behalf or on behalf of Harvard University."Therefore, this clarification is to explain to the larger audience that certain individuals who happen to be alumni of Harvard University have issued the statement in their personal capacity. While we respect personal expression, that is not a substitute for institutional representation," he added.In an official statement, the Club said that a statement reportedly issued by a group of individuals identifying themselves as Harvard University alumni, commenting on police action against protesters and the detention of certain individuals, reflected only the personal views of its signatories.It stated, "This is to clarify that the Harvard Club of India, the officially recognised alumni association representing Harvard University alumni in India, has neither issued nor endorsed any statement concerning the recent protests in New Delhi or the actions taken by the authorities in connection with these events. A statement reportedly issued by a group of individuals identifying themselves as Harvard University alumni, expressing views on the police action against protesters and the detention of certain individuals, represents the personal views of its signatories alone."The Club said the statement should not be construed as its official position or as an institutional endorsement."It should not be construed as reflecting the official position, views, or institutional endorsement of the Harvard Club of India, the statement read.The Harvard Club of India said its governing bylaws do not authorise individuals or groups to make political statements or express positions on behalf of the Club or Harvard University.The Club reiterated its commitment to maintaining a clear distinction between individual expression and official institutional representation.

articles.text:

articles.title: Investors shrug off bear party, put big money into equity mutual funds
articles.text: Mumbai: Equity mutual fund inflows hit a five-month high in September, with investors pouring money into small- and mid-cap schemes despite a weak equity market backdrop and sustained foreign investor selling. Debt funds, however, witnessed outflows, led by redemptions from liquid and money market schemes by companies for advance tax payments, partly resulting in the mutual fund industry posting outflows during the month.Net inflows into equity schemes rose nearly 31% from the prior month to ₹38,306.55 crore in September, extending the momentum seen in August when investments increased nearly 19%, according to data from the Association of Mutual Funds in India. With September's inflows, equity funds have now recorded net inflows for 67 consecutive months.Contributions under monthly systematic investment plans (SIPs) hit a monthly record at ₹32,490 crore in September, up from ₹32,297 crore in August. SIP assets under management rose to ₹17.86 lakh crore.134905091The strong inflows came even as both the Sensex and Nifty indexes declined about 6% during the month on concerns over rising crude oil prices, higher US bond yields and continued selling by foreign portfolio investors.Among equity categories, small-cap funds attracted the highest inflows at ₹9,038.57 crore, followed by mid-cap at ₹7,834.84 crore. Together, the two segments accounted for about 44% of the total inflows into equity funds. Investors continue to favour mid- and small-cap categories despite their relatively weak recent performance, said Viraj Gandhi, CEO of Samco Mutual Fund."The 12-month benchmark performance was mixed as the large-cap index fell 12% and the mid-cap index fell 1%, while the small-cap index rose 3%. Against that backdrop, September's equity-fund flows suggest investors were still favouring mid- and small-cap exposure despite their recent weak performance," Gandhi said.Flexi-cap funds received ₹6,701.80 crore during the month, up from ₹5,059.42 crore in August, while large-cap funds returned to the positive territory with net inflows of ₹859.47 crore after witnessing net outflows of ₹1,147 crore in the previous month.Read more: Jubilant Pharmova block deal: Quant Mutual Fund offloads Rs 190 crore stake amid Rs 800 crore fundraising plan; Abakkus buys 11 lakh sharesHowever, the number of systematic investment plans accounts presented a contrasting picture. Around 6.3 million new SIP accounts were registered last month, while nearly 7.3 million matured or were discontinued, resulting in closures and maturities exceeding fresh registrations by about a million.Debt FundsDebt funds witnessed a sharp reversal, with net outflows surging to ₹1.83 lakh crore in September from ₹8,127.32 crore in August. Liquid funds accounted for the bulk of the withdrawals, recording net outflows of ₹95,743.20 crore compared with inflows of ₹19,934.29 crore in August. Money market funds also saw net outflows of ₹50,846.21 crore after attracting ₹11,734.71 crore in the previous month.The sharp pullback from debt funds dragged the industry's overall flows into the negative territory. The mutual fund industry reported net outflows of ₹1.33 lakh crore in September compared with net inflows of ₹41,368.05 crore in August.Read more: HCL Tech Q2 Results: Profit jumps 21% YoY to Rs 5,132 crore; co declares Rs 12/share dividend"The decline was overwhelmingly driven by liquidity-oriented categories, suggesting quarter-end treasury adjustments and institutional cash-management activity rather than a broad-based deterioration in investor appetite for fixed income," said Nehal Meshram, senior analyst at Morningstar Investment Research India.The industry's total assets under management declined 5.1% to ₹82.64 lakh crore as of September 30 from ₹87.08 lakh crore in August, largely reflecting the sharp outflows from debt-oriented schemes and mark-to-market impact from the fall in equities.Gold ETFs saw monthly inflows of ₹4,451 crore, marking a 71% jump from ₹2,597 crore in August, as investors turned to the safe-haven asset amid geopolitical tensions.

articles.title: Top 10 blue-chips’ share of India’s m-cap drops to lowest since 2017
articles.text: Mumbai: India's top 10 listed blue-chips have steadily lost their share of the country's total market capitalisation, with their combined weight falling to a near-decade low led by sustained foreign portfolio investor (FPI) selling and the underperformance of large-cap stocks.The top 10 companies accounted for around 17.65% of the total market capitalisation of all listed firms as on October 9, a level last seen in January 2017. Their combined market cap stood at ₹84.84 lakh crore, the lowest since December 2023, while the market cap of all listed companies was around ₹480.82 lakh crore till last weekend.Heavy foreign selling has weighed on large-cap stocks.134905140"FPIs have withdrawn above ₹3 lakh crore from Indian secondary markets since the start of 2026, with the top 10 companies accounting for nearly 60-70% of the selling," said Rajesh Singla, CEO and fund manager, Alpha AMC. "A weaker rupee has added to the pressure."The concentration of market value among the country's largest companies has steadily declined over the past few years. The top 10 companies accounted for around 25% of total market capitalisation at the start of 2023, falling to nearly 22% in early 2024 and 21% in January 2025. The share slipped below 20% earlier this year before declining to current levels.Read more: Polycab India’s F&O exit: NSE sets December 30 deadline; NCLAT stays insolvency orderAt the same time, domestic flows have continued to support the broader market. As smaller companies outperformed large-cap stocks, their share as a proportion of the total market cap went up.The combined share of small- and mid-cap companies in the total market capitalisation of listed companies rose to 20.6% and 23.1%, respectively, in September 2026, from around 18% at the start of the year 2024, according to ET calculations."The shift reflects changing investor perceptions about which companies and sectors are best positioned to capture India's next phase of growth," said Swagatam Biswas, head of public equities at Avendus Wealth Management.Read more: Jubilant Pharmova block deal: Quant Mutual Fund offloads Rs 190 crore stake amid Rs 800 crore fundraising plan; Abakkus buys 11 lakh sharesInvestors are looking beyond traditional index heavyweights towards companies benefiting from emerging opportunities, including public infrastructure, he said. "The large-cap fatigue is largely happening due to this," Biswas said.The underperformance of several index heavyweights has contributed to the decline in the top 10 companies' share of total market capitalisation. Reliance Industries, India's largest company by market cap, has declined 26% this year. HDFC Bank and Bharti Airtel have fallen 27% and 15%, respectively, while TCS is down 32%. Larsen & Toubro has declined 11%, LIC 7% and Bajaj Finance 3%. ICICI Bank and State Bank of India have remained broadly flat, while Kotak Mahindra Bank has gained 1%.

articles.title: Microsoft blames a configuration change for Exchange Admin Center tumble
articles.text: Microsoft took down the Exchange Admin Center (EAC) today after a code change left administrators facing an "Internal Server Error" when trying to access the service. Microsoft first admitted that something was amiss at 0937 UTC on October 12, noting, "When attempting to access the Exchange admin center, affected admins may encounter an 'Internal Server Error' message." Any administrator attempting to access the EAC could be affected. It was more than an hour before the company stated: "We've identified unexpected 302 redirect errors during affected Exchange admin center (EAC) access attempts and are analyzing diagnostic logs to isolate the source of the access failures. "While we continue our investigation, admins remain unable to access the EAC, with no workaround currently available." So, a fun morning for Microsoft's European users. According to Microsoft, the EAC is "a modern, web-based management console for managing Exchange Online." Want to manage mailboxes? EAC is where you go. Group management? Again, EAC. Microsoft explained: "The design of the EAC in Exchange Online aligns with the overall Microsoft 365 admin experience." Sadly, that alignment appears to extend to service wobbles caused by changes rolled out without due care and attention. Two hours after admitting things had gone awry, Microsoft said it was "continuing to test the rollback of the recent Exchange admin center (EAC) change while monitoring the results to determine if this resolves the impact." At this point, administrators were nodding sagely at an all-too familiar story. Of course rolling back the change did the trick. Microsoft stated as much in its final update: "A recent EAC configuration change resulted in unexpected HTTP responses within the affected request path, preventing admins from successfully accessing the EAC. "Reverting the identified change restored expected service functionality." Microsoft also assured customers it was reviewing the change to ensure it didn't make the same mistake again, as well as its monitoring and telemetry, to "improve detection and alerting for similar service behavior." The problem is that this is hardly a new phenomenon. In September, Microsoft made a configuration change that left some users unable to access SharePoint Online sites and pages. In April, another ill-thought-through change took down Outlook for iOS. And, in 2025, Microsoft 365 tumbled from the cloud because of yet another configuration change. It's almost as if testing changes consists of little more than asking Copilot, "does this look alright to you?" and then hitting the go button. The latest outage was resolved before the end of the working day, and a preliminary Post-Incident Report is due within two business days, with a final report due next week. Hopefully one or the other will contain words along the lines of "Hey, this keeps happening, maybe we should do some more testing before deploying to production?" ®

articles.title: Chatbot refuseniks edge out users in the US, and they’re not for turning
articles.text: If you thought everyone was into chatbots, think again: about half of US adults never use the AI tools, and most have no interest in starting. According to Pew Research Center, older adults are the least likely to use chatbots, with roughly three-quarters of those aged 65 and older saying they never use them. That may be expected, yet more than half (58 percent) of adults aged 50 to 64 don't use them either. Those aged 18 to 29 use chatbots the most, at 66 percent, however even a third of them say they never do. About four in ten under 50 report not using them at all. Across all adults, 51 percent are chatbot refuseniks, so users are - just barely - the minority. Pew asked non-users to choose from five possible reasons. Six in ten cited simple lack of interest as a major factor, followed by the more familiar concerns of data privacy and the accuracy of chatbot answers. Some Reg readers might suspect older people avoid chatbots because they lack tech-savviness, but fewer than a third cited not knowing how to use them as a major reason. The authors of the survey also found fewer than one in five worried about what others might think of them for using the technology, so social stigma isn’t the deterrent either. Adoption also differs by race and ethnicity: non-users are more likely to be white, black or hispanic than Asian, according to Pew’s survey. The AI dodgers don't look ready to budge. Two-thirds (67 percent) say they’re unlikely to use the technology in the next 12 months, including 40 percent who say they’re not at all likely to change their mind. Another 12 percent are unsure, and just 5 percent of non-users think they'll probably try a chatbot over the next year. Perhaps abstainers were put off by a bad experience, such as Microsoft’s notorious racist chatbot Tay a decade ago. Or something more recent, like the Trump administration’s official America.gov service, which at the time of writing still displays a hotdog if you type that into the prompt. ®

articles.title: No shame in the Domain Name game: DNS is doomed, literally
articles.text: What is DNS? That's right, it's a database. You can disagree with me but you would be wrong. What can you put in a database? Strings, ints (and you learn the difference right quick if your AWS account ID has a leading zero!), JSON objects, coordinates; some of the databases out there have some pretty esoteric types. PostgreSQL supports circle, a polygon, a macaddr8, and a tsquery. Oracle will store a ROWID and your dignity. In a word, databases store data. Can you put answers in a database? Well sure; you could record that "3 + 2 is equal to 5" and store that answer. You can do the same with comparison operators; "3 is larger than 2" and so on. Take it a step further and you've built something with your database: a remarkably inconvenient calculator. So now we've established that you can store arithmetic and decisions in a database. And what can we do with those things? That's right, we can follow instructions! Good job! And what does following instructions require? Generally, memory; a place to store your numbers, your instructions, and which instruction comes next. If only we had a place to store those things. Oh right, we do; we have a database! Now connect those lookups together. Read an instruction, look up an answer, save the result, repeat as needed. So what have we built? That's right: a computer! And what can a computer run? Programs! My, you're quite good at this. And now, gentle reader: what program do we apparently have a moral obligation to run on every computer? Oh yes, though many of you are going to sit back and instead say "oh no" as the horror courses through you. I am talking about Doom. This very publication agrees with me! What have I done? That's right; I have compiled Doom for a 32-bit machine whose arithmetic and memory live in DNS. A small program supplies the wiring and the clock, neither of which the architects of DNS saw fit to include. But DNS does supply the answers. So, can we play Doom? Only if it's turn-based. It won't render on human timescales anyway. In my first attempt, I pressed Right, and then waited for 577 seconds to find out what happened. By using native transport, pipelining, packing registers densely, and optimizing instruction blocks, I was able to drop that to 146 seconds, before I hit a wall. BIND answers in about 7 µs per query over TCP and 4 µs over UDP, which is fast. The problem is that a 32-bit add is four DNS lookups, a branch is five, and a frame needs 6.6 million of them, so don't use a server that charges per request. And what do we do when BIND isn't performing the way we want it to? I don't know what you do, but I publish my code, then reach out to Paul Vixie, DNS pioneer and architect of BIND 8 to unjustifiably complain. Paul then apparently congratulates me on "the best use of RFC 2136 DNS UPDATE" that he'd ever seen. Given that he's a co-author of that RFC, I suspect he's seen a lot! Which was gratifying, but unhelpful. So let's take another crack at it. What if I do lookaheads? Good thought, bad outcome, because BIND is bound by message count, not chain depth. Well okay, I have some more tricks in my Big Bag of Stupid Ideas. So I went a bit further and via committing registers to DNS less often, moving lookups to UDP, telling BIND to stop padding answers with authority records, and requiring fewer lookups per instruction, I was ultimately able to get that press-right time down from 577 seconds to 146.3 seconds to 54.4 seconds, for a 10.6x improvement. And now I think I have hit a wall. Even at one DNS exchange per instruction (which is far better than anything realistically achievable), 1.4 million instructions at roughly 10 µs each is 14 seconds per tick. Doom says its tic rate is 35 per second, so "playable" is a tic every 28.6 ms. I remain at 54,000 ms, which is three orders of magnitude away from victory. Okay seriously, WHAT? This legitimately works. Every commit is an RFC 2136 UPDATE with a hard requirement: it fails unless the previous state is still exactly what was last written. Apparently "real" database people call that optimistic concurrency, or compare-and-swap. Joke's on you, friends; DNS has shipped with that since 1997; has your inferior database? The database itself is 6.4 million rows of truth tables. ff.01.0.add holds "001": 255 plus 1 is 00 carry 1. DNS is just acting as a librarian here, fetching memorized answers to any arithmetic question in-scope and returning the answer upon request. It's also verifiable! The frame that's spat out is checked on every pixel against an independent emulator. If one record is corrupted in the AND table, the answer changes, which proves there's no local fallback doing arithmetic for us. I've included tooling so that reviewers can run two commands against that repo and verify correctness. I also confess I cheated slightly here; the run I'm pulling these numbers from started from a checkpoint prepared by a normal emulator. It turns out that for SOME UNKNOWN REASON getting a cold boot through Doom's startup screens via DNS would take hours. Also, before the timer starts, DNS has to load those 6.4 million records, so it's a computer that takes roughly a minute to boot before it can even start. We can't cheat This runs atop nothing special: Debian's stock BIND 9.20, configured through named.conf. It lives in a container with networking disabled. I want to be very clear here: this isn't DNS pretending to be a CPU. The instruction decoding is done ahead of time by a compiler; BIND never executes an instruction itself. All that it sees is a key-value read, a conditional write, and 6.4 million rows of precomputed answers. So instead, think of this monstrosity as a database with a key-value read, a conditional write, and 6.4 million rows of precomputed answers. It's not really a computer; it's simply a very good database. And that turns out to be enough. ®

articles.title: Reasoning-Token Spikes Under Prompted Untruthful Responses in Large Language Models
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.10405v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Monitoring the chain-of-thought of reasoning artificial intelligence (AI) models remains a key approach to detecting deception and other forms of misbehavior in such models. However, semantic chain-of-thought monitoring depends on reasoning traces being legible and sufficiently faithful to the underlying computations that produced the model's behavior, not to mention accessible. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that chain-of-thought outputs may soon become illegible or unfaithful, if they even remain accessible. Based on cognitive load theory, we investigate a lower-bandwidth signal--the number of reasoning tokens generated--which does not require access to the content of the reasoning trace. Three reasoning-capable large language models answered 210 multiple-choice questions--across analytic, descriptive, and normative reasoning types as well as moral and non-moral domains--under system prompts instructing them to respond truthfully, falsely, or without regard for truth. Across all three models, truth-directed responses elicited fewer reasoning tokens than both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responses. In addition, in one model, untruthful instructions increased the likelihood of reasoning at all. These findings show that explicitly prompted untruthful response policies can produce robust group-level differences in test-time reasoning-token use. While not yet establishing reasoning-token count as a detector of spontaneous deception or general misalignment, our results are a proof of concept that it can serve as a simple, content-independent black-box candidate signal for differentiating untruthful from truthful model behavior when raw reasoning traces are unavailable or unreliable. Future work should test instance-level detection rates, out-of-distribution generalization, learned deceptive policies, hidden objectives, and robustness under adversarial pressure.

articles.title: Exploring More, Reasoning Better: Stepwise Risk-Sensitive GRPO for Diffusion Language Models
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.00661v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by denoising a sequence or successive blocks, allowing several tokens to be revealed in parallel. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reuses terminal feedback across these decisions, even as their conditioning context changes. We propose stepwise risk-sensitive GRPO (StepRS-GRPO), which varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, we show that this transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection. Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. In our ablation studies, mass-matched controls support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and the gains persist after matching the root mean square (RMS) of the advantages to that of centered GRPO. Reasoning-trace diagnostics further show that the diversity gains from StepRS-GRPO extend beyond final-answer strings.
